dervis-irab:1-5.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْفَلَقِ): the dawn. al-Zamakhsharī said: "al-Falaq and al-Faraq are the dawn, because the night is split (yafliq) and divided (yafriq) from it; it is a form faʿal in the sense of mafʿūl. It is said in the proverb: 'He is clearer than the split of the dawn (falaq al-ṣubḥ) and than the division of the dawn (faraq al-ṣubḥ)', and from it is their saying 'the roof shone with the furqān' when the dawn rose." The poet said:
يا ليلة لم أنمها بتّ مرتقبا ... أرعى النجوم إلى أن قدر الفلق
(O night in which I did not sleep, I spent it watching, tending the stars until the dawn was decreed.)
And another, describing the wild bull:
حتى إذا ما انجلى عن وجهه فلق ... هاديه في أخريات الليل منتصب
(Until, when a daybreak cleared from its face, its guide stood erect in the last parts of the night.)
There are other views on what is meant by it, to be referred to in the longer works; the first is preferable, and so we have passed them over.
(غاسِقٍ): al-ghāsiq is the night when its darkness thickens. The poet said:
يا طيف هند لقد أبقيت لي أرقا ... إذ جئتنا طارقا والليل قد غسقا
(O phantom of Hind, you have left me sleepless, when you came to us by night, as the night had darkened.)
(وَقَبَ): its darkness entered everything. It is said "the sun waqabat" when it set. In the ḥadīth: "When he saw that the sun had waqabat", he said, "This is when it becomes permissible", meaning the evening prayer. There are other views, not suited to this place.
(النَّفَّاثاتِ): the sorceresses who blow upon the knots they tie. al-nafth, as in al-Mukhtār, is "similar to blowing (nafkh) but less than spitting (tafl); the reciter of charms has blown (nafatha), of the pattern ḍaraba and naṣara; and al-naffāthāt fī l-ʿuqad are the sorceresses." More of its meaning will come in the section on benefits.

* I'rab:
(قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ مِنْ شَرِّ ما خَلَقَ) قل is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; the clause أعوذ is the quoted speech (maqūl al-qawl); أعوذ is an imperfect verb, nominative, its agent latent, its implied form being "I"; برب الفلق is attached to أعوذ, and من شر is attached to أعوذ; ما is a relative noun, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive), and the clause خلق is the ṣila, the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e. "He created it"; it may also be maṣdariyya. (وَمِنْ شَرِّ غاسِقٍ إِذا وَقَبَ) is conjoined to what precedes; إذا is an adverb of mere time reference, and the clause وقب is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it. (وَمِنْ شَرِّ النَّفَّاثاتِ فِي الْعُقَدِ) is likewise conjoined to what precedes, and في العقد is attached to النفاثات. (وَمِنْ شَرِّ حاسِدٍ إِذا حَسَدَ) is conjoined to what precedes, and its i'rab is evident.

* Benefits:
Some of what is sought refuge from is made definite and some indefinite, for generality and for specification: every blowing sorceress is evil, whereas envy is partly praiseworthy and partly blameworthy. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no envy except in two cases," and Abū Tammām said: "Loftiness is beautiful, and in the like of it envy is fine," and he said: "A man envious in noble deeds is not truly an envier."
